ruling_text:
The Court intends to deny Lanise Ward's motion to vacate or modify order of 7/9/25.

1. Failure to Give Notice of Petition to Administer Estate. Probate Code section 8110 provides:
"At least 15 days before the hearing of a petition for administration of a decedent's estate, the petitioner shall deliver notice of the hearing pursuant to Section 1215 on all of the following persons:
(a) Each heir of the decedent, so far as known to or reasonably ascertainable by the petitioner.
(b) Each devisee, executor, and alternative executor named in any will being offered for probate, regardless of whether the devise or appointment is purportedly revoked in a subsequent instrument."
The moving party, Lanise Ward, admits that she was not an heir or devisee of the estate. Since decedent died intestate, she was also not an executor named in any will. Accordingly, the Court finds that she was not entitled to receive a notice of petition to administer estate. (Prob. Code., § 8110.)

2. Interested Person. Ms. Ward contends that she was entitled to receive notice of petition to administer estate as an "interested person" under Probate Code section 48. Section 48, subdivision (a), defines "interested person" to include "any person having a property right in or claim against … the estate of the decedent which may be affected by the proceeding." Although section 48 defines an "interested person," it does not require that an interested person be given notice of petition to administer estate. Again, section 8110 generally governs who must be given notice of petition to administer estate, and it does not include "interested persons."

3. Notice under Prob. Code § 851 and § 1260. The Court finds no merit to Ms. Ward's contention that she was entitled to notice under Probate Code section 851 and section 1260. No 850 petition was filed in this case prior to the final distribution. Section 1260 governs proof of giving notice; it imposes no duty to give notice.

4. Code Civ. Proc., § 473, subd. (b). "A party who seeks relief under section 473 on the basis of mistake or inadvertence of counsel must demonstrate that such mistake, inadvertence, or general neglect was excusable because the negligence of the attorney is imputed to his client and may not be offered by the latter as a basis for relief." (Generale Bank Nederland v. Eyes of the Beholder Ltd. (1998) 61 Cal.App.4th 1384, 1399.) "Excusable neglect is that neglect which might have been the act of a reasonably prudent person under the same circumstances." (Alderman v. Jacobs (1954) 128 Cal.App.2d 273, 276; see also Huh v. Wang (2007) 158 Cal.App.4th 1406, 1419.)
Relevant factors in assessing counsel error include: "(1) the nature of the mistake or neglect; and (2) whether counsel was otherwise diligent in investigating and pursuing the claim." (Bettencourt v. Los Rios Community College Dist. (1986) 42 Cal.3d 270, 276.) "Conduct falling below the professional standard of care, such as failure to timely object or to properly advance an argument, is not therefore excusable." (Garcia v. Hejmadi (1997) 58 Cal.App.4th 674, 682.)

Ms. Ward alleges that her absence from the 7/9/25 hearing on the petition for final distribution was caused solely by the administrator's failure to give legally required notice. But again, Ward has not shown that she was legally entitled to notice of any of the proceedings in this administration.

Chief among the moving party's contentions is that she and her counsel, Lyle Middleton, had no knowledge of this probate case until it was, apparently, too late to appear at the 7/9/25 hearing on the petition for final distribution. However, as she and her counsel are aware, and the Court takes judicial notice of pursuant to Evidence Code section 452, subdivision (d), Ms. Ward was named as a defendant in a civil complaint filed on 1/21/25 in Case No. 2025CUOR037324. Ms. Ward was personally served with a copy of the complaint on 3/25/25. The civil complaint clearly identified Plaintiff Chris Dowd as the administrator of the estate of Christopher Otto Dowd. In this motion, Ms. Ward also admits that as of 3/25/25, she was aware that Chris Dowd was the administrator of his father's probate estate.

Further, the Opposition attaches a letter dated 12/23/24 from Chris Dowd/Josh Oxley's counsel, Stewart Levin, addressed to Ms. Ward and attached to an email sent to her counsel Mr. Middleton on 12/23/24. The letter states in part: "Chris Dowd, sole beneficiary and administrator of the decedent's estate of Christopher Otto Dowd, whom this office represents, is a co-owner of the real property located at 445 Millard Street Moorpark, CA 93021 (the "Property"), holding a [50 %] undivided interest as a tenant in common along with you." The purpose of the letter appears to have been to ask for Ms. Ward's cooperation in a partition sale of the Millard property. In any event, the letter clearly informed and gave notice to both Ms. Ward and Mr. Middleton of the fact that Chris Dowd was the administrator of his father's estate and was claiming to own 50% of the Millard property as a cotenant.

Ms. Ward and her counsel do not explain why, between 12/23/24 and 7/9/25, she did not appear in the probate proceeding to make her claim to the Millard property. Why did she sit on her rights only to claim now that she was wrongly deprived of her opportunity to challenge the petition for final distribution or file claims?

The Court also does not understand why Ms. Ward feels it necessary to file an 850 petition in this case. The Court notes that in the civil action, she filed a cross-complaint alleging various claims against Chris Dowd, including a cause of action for adverse possession. The 850 petition she seeks to file in this case appears duplicative of the claim she is litigating in the civil action.

Based on the foregoing, the Court will deny the motion to vacate or modify.
